title: Estimating Area with Slices
lede: When a quantity changes, slicing it into thin rectangles turns a hard question into arithmetic.

cards.heading: The Question
cards.body: How much area sits between a curve and the x-axis over an interval? For a constant height it is just length times width, but a curve changes height at every point. The fix is to freeze the curve for a moment, treat that height as constant over a tiny slice, and add the slices up.

cards.heading: Riemann Sums
cards.body: Cut the interval from a to b into n equal pieces, so each has width Delta x = (b-a)/n. On each piece pick a sample point, draw a rectangle of that height, and add all n rectangles. Left endpoints undershoot an increasing curve and overshoot a decreasing one; more, thinner rectangles shrink the error either way.

cards.heading: A Worked Slice
cards.body: Estimate the area under f(x) = x^2 on [0, 2] using 4 rectangles with right endpoints. Delta x = 0.5 and the sample heights are 0.25, 1, 2.25, and 4, giving a sum of 3.75. The exact answer is 8/3, about 2.67, so the overestimate is already shrinking as rectangles get thinner.

flashcards.explain: Adds n rectangle areas of width Delta x and heights sampled from the curve. As n grows the sum approaches the exact area under the curve between a and b.
Dividing the interval length by n gives equal slice widths. Smaller Delta x means thinner rectangles and a tighter approximation of the curved region.

flashcards.meaning: The limit that defines the integral
flashcards.explain: Letting the number of rectangles go to infinity while each width goes to zero removes the sampling error. That limit is exactly what the definite integral computes.

mcq.prompt: Using right endpoints to approximate an increasing function with rectangles always produces what kind of estimate?
choices: An underestimate, because the curve rises after each sample point
An overestimate, because the curve rises after each sample point
An exact value, since right endpoints capture the trend
It depends on whether the function is positive
mcq.rightExplain: On each slice an increasing function is highest at its right edge, so the rectangle covers a little extra area and the sum overshoots.
mcq.wrongExplain: Left endpoints undershoot increasing curves, and positivity affects the sign of the sum but not whether right endpoints run high on a rising curve.

topic: The definite integral and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
title: Antiderivatives Unlock the Integral
lede: The Fundamental Theorem says the two great ideas of calculus, slopes and areas, are inverse operations.

cards.heading: Defining the Integral
cards.body: The definite integral of f from a to b is the limit of Riemann sums as the slices get infinitely thin. It measures signed area: regions above the axis count positive, regions below count negative. A function can be negative everywhere and still have a perfectly good, negative integral.

cards.heading: FTC Part 1
cards.body: Define an area-so-far function by integrating f from a fixed point a up to a variable endpoint x. Differentiate that accumulation and you get back f itself. This is the theorem's first half: integration, run forward, is undone by differentiation.

cards.heading: FTC Part 2
cards.body: The second half says you can evaluate a definite integral with any antiderivative F: the answer is F(b) minus F(a), no limits required. For f(x) = x^2 on [0, 2], an antiderivative is x^3/3, so the integral is 8/3 minus 0. What took an infinite sum by hand is now two evaluations.

flashcards.meaning: Evaluation form of the Fundamental Theorem
flashcards.explain: If F is any antiderivative of f, the definite integral equals the antiderivative evaluated at the endpoints and subtracted. This bypasses computing Riemann sums entirely.
The accumulation function grows at exactly the rate f supplies area. Differentiating the integral with a variable upper limit returns the original integrand.
The integral tracks accumulated change, so it answers with net results. Distance traveled uses speed, not velocity, because direction reversals would cancel otherwise.

mcq.prompt: A car's velocity is v(t) = 2t for 0 to 3 seconds. What does the integral of v from 0 to 3 give, and what is its value?
mcq.rightExplain: Integrating velocity gives displacement, and an antiderivative t^2 evaluated from 0 to 3 yields 9. The units work out to meters.
mcq.wrongExplain: Integrating velocity does not give average velocity or acceleration, and 18 comes from forgetting that the antiderivative of 2t is t^2, not 2t^2.

title: Reversing the Chain Rule
lede: An indefinite integral is the family of all antiderivatives, and u-substitution is the chain rule read backwards.

cards.heading: Antiderivatives
cards.body: The indefinite integral of f is any function whose derivative is f, written with a C because derivatives cannot see constants. If F works, then F plus any constant also works, so the answer is a family, not a single function. Basic rules mirror differentiation: powers, exponentials, and sines each reverse cleanly.

cards.heading: The Substitution Idea
cards.body: When an integrand contains a function and (a multiple of) its derivative, the chain rule is hiding inside. Pick u to be the inner function so that du covers the leftover factor. The integral then collapses to a basic form in u, you integrate, and substitute back at the end.

cards.heading: A Worked Swap
cards.body: Take the integral of x times the square root of (1 + x^2). Let u = 1 + x^2, so du = 2x dx and the x dx becomes du/2. The integral is now one half the integral of u to the one half power, which gives u to the three halves over three, so the final answer is (1 + x^2) to the three halves over 3 plus C.

flashcards.explain: Every antiderivative is known only up to a constant, since the derivative of a constant is zero. Omitting C makes an indefinite integral answer technically wrong.
Choosing u triggers a matching replacement for dx. The substituted integral must contain no stray x terms, or the choice of u needs adjusting.
Every power except negative one integrates by the power rule. The exponent negative one lands on the natural logarithm instead, and the absolute value keeps the domain safe.

mcq.prompt: To evaluate the integral of 2x times e to the (x squared), what substitution fits best?
choices: u = 2x, since the coefficient is out front
u = e^x, to simplify the exponential
u = x^2, since du = 2x dx matches the leftover factor
No substitution is needed; integrate directly by parts
mcq.rightExplain: With u = x^2, du = 2x dx absorbs the outside factor exactly, leaving the elementary integral of e to the u.
mcq.wrongExplain: Taking u = 2x leaves e to the x squared still tangled in x, and integration by parts is unnecessary when a clean du = 2x dx is already sitting there.
